record.paper_title: Finite-density lattice QCD and sign problem: current status and open problems
record.original_question: Can quantum entanglement or tensor-network-based descriptions provide a genuinely new route to solving or sharply characterizing the sign problem in finite-density QCD? More specifically, can entanglement serve as the right measure of the effective degrees of freedom and computational cost in a way that leads to new numerical strategies for dense QCD?

evidence.quote: Quantum entanglement may be a good characterization of the computational cost.
Such a new viewpoint may lead to the solution of the sign problem.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider lattice quantum chromodynamics (lattice QCD) at nonzero baryon chemical potential μ ≠ 0. The Euclidean fermion determinant det M(μ) is generally complex, so the standard Boltzmann weight e^{-S_g} det M(μ) cannot be interpreted as a probability density. This obstruction—the sign problem—prevents direct importance-sampling Monte Carlo simulation of dense QCD, including the quark–gluon plasma, nuclear matter, and neutron-star regimes.

A tensor-network state on a lattice is a variational ansatz (e.g. matrix product state, projected entangled pair state, MERA) for the wavefunction or path-integral tensor, parametrized by local tensors whose bond dimension D controls the maximal bipartite entanglement entropy S ≤ log D that the ansatz can represent. Tensor-network methods are formulated directly in Hilbert space (or as exact tensor contractions of the partition function) and therefore do not rely on probabilistic sampling of complex weights, so they are not afflicted by the sign problem in the Monte Carlo sense.

Question. Determine whether quantum entanglement and tensor-network representations can provide a genuinely new route to solving or sharply characterizing the sign problem of finite-density lattice QCD in 3+1 dimensions. In particular:

(a) Does the bipartite entanglement entropy of the ground state (or thermal state) of finite-density QCD serve as a faithful measure of the effective number of degrees of freedom and of the computational cost required by any tensor-network algorithm that targets that state? Make this notion precise and prove or disprove it.

(b) Construct, or prove the impossibility of constructing, a tensor-network algorithm whose computational cost (as a function of system size, lattice spacing, and chemical potential) is polynomial in the relevant entanglement measure and which yields controlled approximations to expectation values of gauge-invariant observables in 3+1-dimensional lattice QCD at nonzero baryon density.
artifact.category_tag: lattice QCD sign problem and tensor networks
artifact.status_search_result: Recent literature (2024–2025) confirms that tensor-network methods are intrinsically free of the Monte Carlo sign problem and have been successfully applied to low-dimensional lattice gauge theories, with progress in 2+1D SU(2) and steps toward higher dimensions, but a tensor-network solution of finite-density lattice QCD in 3+1D remains out of reach. Whether entanglement provides the correct measure of computational cost for dense QCD is still an open research direction.

status_evidence.title: Tensor networks for lattice gauge theories beyond one dimension
status_evidence.snippet: Tensor networks are intrinsically sign-problem-free... progress beyond 1D remains challenging.
status_evidence.claim: Tensor networks are sign-problem-free but extending to higher-dimensional gauge theories such as full QCD is an active, unresolved research program.

status_evidence.title: Towards overcoming the Monte Carlo sign problem with tensor networks
status_evidence.snippet: Tensor networks offer a route to overcome the sign problem; demonstrated in low-dimensional models.
status_evidence.claim: Tensor networks have been demonstrated as a sign-problem-free approach in lower-dimensional gauge models, but full finite-density QCD has not been solved.

status_evidence.title: Accurate Ground States of SU(2) Lattice Gauge Theory
status_evidence.snippet: Tensor-network ground states for SU(2) lattice gauge theory in 2+1D.
status_evidence.claim: State of the art reaches 2+1D SU(2); 3+1D finite-density QCD via tensor networks remains open.
